newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: SOCCER-GOAL-SHY AJAX MIRED IN MEDIOCRITY.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-GOAL-SHY AJAX MIRED IN MEDIOCRITY.

text.p: An exuberant blend of talent, youth and intelligence promised to usher in "an orange future" but Ajax Amsterdam, who strutted the European stage for two glorious seasons, have lost their shine.
The 1995 world and European champions, dethroned by Juventus last season only in a penalty shoot-out, have spluttered and wheezed and already look out of the reckoning for major titles.

Ripped apart by the Bosman ruling on freedom of movement for out-of-contract players and uncomfortable in a 21st century palace of a stadium, the Dutch champions are in danger of slipping back among Europe's also-rans.
The club's philosophy remains undimmed but injuries and transfers have taken their toll, while some mutter darkly about the move to a towering multi-million guilder stadium.
The impressive Arena, built to house the cream of European soccer, is currently playing host to mid-table mediocrity.
The pitch is worn and hampers Ajax's fluid style, while fans lament the absence of history and air of invincibility which the club had in their old cramped headquarters at De Meer.

After a miserable pre-season Ajax have failed to fire in the domestic campaign. Ten games into the championship, they are sixth in the first division, sandwiched between Roda JC Kerkrade and Vitesse Arnhem with just 16 points.
A 1-0 away win at Auxerre in the European Cup Champions' League opener raised hopes that Ajax's dismal early league form was misleading.
But defeat at home to Grasshopper Zurich in the second encounter means they have no guarantee of a place in the last eight of Europe's premier club competition.
More pertinently, Ajax have scored only 10 league goals. And that, observers say, is the crux of their malaise.
The Ajax machine continues to create chances, though not quite as fluently as in the past two seasons, but it has lost the killer touch in front of goal.

Patrick Kluivert is sidelined with a knee ligament injury which will keep him out until November. Nigerian fellow striker Nwankwo Kanu, whose career is now threatened by a heart defect, has gone to Italy -- and the goals have dried up.
Marc Overmars, who, on song, is one of the best wingers in Europe, is a shadow of the classy player he was before a knee injury forced him into a long lay-off.

Finn Jari Litmanen, scorer of 19 European Cup goals, has carried injuries and lost confidence, while midfield motor Edgar Davids was given away to AC Milan in the close season, one of four stalwarts sacrificed to the Bosman effect.
Replacements, such as Dutch internationals Richard Witschge and Peter Hoekstra, Argentine Ivan Gabrich and Brazil's Mariano Juan, have all been dogged by injury.
Hoekstra faces a knee operation this week and is expected to be out for most of the rest of the season.

Nigerian Tijjani Babangida, signed from Roda JC to replace Spain-bound Finidi George, has looked ill at ease in the rarefied atmosphere of the Ajax camp. One glaring miss against Grasshopper seemed to sum up his early contribution.
Skipper Danny Blind, 35, nears the end of a distinguished career and, around him, the defence has had to adjust to the loss of Michael Reiziger, another who left for Italy's serie A.
Blind said last week he was having a groin operation and would miss up to three months of the season.
As the injuries mount up, Dutch national physiotherapist Frits Kessel has called for a smaller first division to allow players to recover and train properly between matches.
"We've gone beyond what players should have to endure," he said. "Look at Ajax. They have a sensible policy (on resting injured players) but there is a risk attached. It costs points."
Dick van Gangelen of the Dutch daily Algemeen Dagblad says the number of injuries is the key to Ajax's decline:
"They are forced to change the team every week, so they never get used to playing the system they want to play like they did last year when, with their eyes closed, everybody knew what to do."
Coach Louis van Gaal, architect of Ajax's most recent triumphs, said last week he would leave the club at the end of the season.
Van Gaal took over as coach from Leo Beenhakker in September 1991 and led the club to three Dutch titles, the European Cup and UEFA Cup as well as assorted Dutch, Super and other cups.
The Dutch media said Johan Cruyff was emerging as favourite to take over as coach next season at the club he guided, as a player, to three European Cup triumphs in the early 1970s.
Cruyff, coach at Ajax from 1985 to 1988, was sacked by Barcelona earlier this year after after eight years in charge of the Spanish club.
